description: Whole-body composite phenotype dimensions: Heath-Carter somatotype, body composition pattern, proportions, frame size, musculature, posture, and lower-limb alignment. This category absorbs the original Height, Weight, Limb, and Knees atlas categories by treating them as composite-body measures rather than discrete body parts. Dimensions are drawn from sports-medicine, public-health, and anthropometric literature. Most dimensions require full-body framing to assess; height and weight require measurement and are flagged not_assessable from photographs.

dimensions.scale_citation: Carter JEL, Heath BH (1990). Somatotyping — Development and Applications. Cambridge University Press.
dimensions.description: Relative degree of fatness — the endomorphic component of the Heath-Carter somatotype. Higher values indicate greater subcutaneous fat envelope. Originally measured from skinfold sites; visual estimation from photograph correlates moderately.

values.definition: Minimal subcutaneous fat; bony landmarks prominent throughout the trunk and limbs.
Average subcutaneous fat envelope; soft-tissue coverage of skeletal landmarks.
Pronounced subcutaneous fat envelope; bony landmarks substantially obscured.

observability.notes: Visual estimation correlates moderately with skinfold-measured values. Treat as soft estimate; ground-truth measurement requires three skinfold sites (triceps, subscapular, supraspinale).

dimensions.scale_citation: Carter JEL, Heath BH (1990). Somatotyping — Development and Applications. Cambridge University Press.
dimensions.description: Relative musculoskeletal robustness — the mesomorphic component of the Heath-Carter somatotype. Higher values indicate greater muscle mass and skeletal robustness relative to height.

values.definition: Slight musculoskeletal development; narrow bone structure.
Average muscle mass and skeletal robustness.
Pronounced muscle mass and robust skeletal frame.

observability.notes: Originally measured from bone breadths and limb girths corrected for skinfold; visual estimation reasonably accurate.

dimensions.scale_citation: Carter JEL, Heath BH (1990). Somatotyping — Development and Applications. Cambridge University Press.
dimensions.description: Relative linearity — the ectomorphic component of the Heath-Carter somatotype. Higher values indicate greater height-for-mass and a more linear physique.

values.definition: Compact, low height-for-mass.
Average linearity.
Highly linear; long-limbed; high height-for-mass.

observability.notes: Computed from height-to-cube-root-of-weight ratio (HWR); visual estimation captures the perceptual linearity correlate.

dimensions.scale_citation: Carter JEL, Heath BH (1990). Somatotyping — Development and Applications. Cambridge University Press.
dimensions.description: Single-label summary of Heath-Carter somatotype based on which component dominates. Derived from the three component scores; included as a discrete categorical for cross-group comparison.

values.definition: All three components within one unit of each other; no single dominance.
Endomorphy dominant; mesomorphy and ectomorphy approximately equal and lower.
Endomorphy dominant; mesomorphy second.
Endomorphy and mesomorphy approximately equal and dominant; ectomorphy lower.
Mesomorphy dominant; endomorphy second.
Mesomorphy dominant; endomorphy and ectomorphy approximately equal and lower.
Mesomorphy dominant; ectomorphy second.
Mesomorphy and ectomorphy approximately equal and dominant; endomorphy lower.
Ectomorphy dominant; mesomorphy second.
Ectomorphy dominant; endomorphy and mesomorphy approximately equal and lower.
Ectomorphy dominant; endomorphy second.
Endomorphy and ectomorphy approximately equal and dominant; mesomorphy lower.
Endomorphy dominant; ectomorphy second.

observability.notes: Derived from the three component scores. The model can either output this directly or it can be computed downstream from the three component values.

dimensions.scale_citation: Standard anthropometric stature measurement; standing height from sole to vertex.
dimensions.description: Stature in centimeters. Requires direct measurement; not derivable from a single photograph without a calibrated reference object. Included for structured-text use cases (clinical records, athlete databases) where measured values are available.

observability.notes: A photograph alone does not yield reliable height estimates. The dimension is included so external measured values can populate it through structured-text ingestion.

dimensions.description: Body mass in kilograms. Requires direct measurement; not derivable from a photograph. Included for structured-text use cases.

dimensions.scale_citation: WHO (2000). Obesity: preventing and managing the global epidemic. WHO Technical Report Series 894. Asian-Pacific thresholds: WHO Expert Consultation (2004), The Lancet, 363(9403): 157-163.
dimensions.description: WHO BMI category, ordinal. Asian-Pacific population BMI thresholds are lower than the WHO universal thresholds because of higher body-fat percentage at equivalent BMI in those populations; the scale lists both anchor points where they differ.

values.definition: BMI < 16.0 kg/m².
BMI 18.5–24.9 kg/m² (WHO universal); 18.5–22.9 kg/m² (Asian-Pacific).
BMI 25.0–29.9 kg/m² (WHO universal); 23.0–27.4 kg/m² (Asian-Pacific).
BMI 30.0–34.9 kg/m² (WHO universal); 27.5–32.4 kg/m² (Asian-Pacific).
BMI 35.0–39.9 kg/m² (WHO universal); 32.5–37.4 kg/m² (Asian-Pacific).
BMI ≥ 40.0 kg/m² (WHO universal); ≥ 37.5 kg/m² (Asian-Pacific).

observability.notes: Visual estimation of BMI from a photograph is unreliable across the normal-overweight boundary. Treat as soft estimate at coarse buckets only (e.g. underweight / normal / overweight / obese — without subdividing obese classes from a photo).

dimensions.scale_citation: WHO (2008). Waist Circumference and Waist-Hip Ratio: Report of a WHO Expert Consultation. Singh D (1993). Adaptive significance of female physical attractiveness: role of waist-to-hip ratio. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 65(2): 293-307.
dimensions.description: Visual-estimate categorization of waist-to-hip ratio. Sex-specific clinical thresholds (≥0.85 women, ≥0.90 men) indicate elevated cardiometabolic risk; this scale is a qualitative-bucket equivalent for visual assessment.

values.definition: Waist substantially narrower than hips; hourglass-equivalent silhouette.
Waist clearly narrower than hips but not pronounced.
Waist approximates or exceeds hip width; rectangular or apple-shaped silhouette.

observability.notes: Frontal view sufficient; clothing affects accuracy.

dimensions.scale_citation: Anthropometric proportional reasoning; relative biacromial-to-biiliac breadth used in sports-medicine and aesthetic-anatomy contexts.
dimensions.description: Relative breadth of the hips compared to the shoulders. A secondary sex characteristic that varies by ethnic group and sex.

values.definition: Inverted-triangle silhouette; biacromial breadth substantially exceeds biiliac breadth.
Approximately equal hip and shoulder breadth.
Pear-shaped silhouette; biiliac breadth approaches or exceeds biacromial breadth.

dimensions.scale_citation: Frisancho AR (1984). New standards of weight and body composition by frame size and height for assessment of nutritional status of adults and the elderly. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 40(4): 808-819. Grant JP, DeHoog S (1985). Nutritional Assessment in Clinical Care.
dimensions.description: Skeletal frame size, qualitative bucket. Originally measured by elbow breadth or wrist circumference; visual estimation captures the silhouette correlate. Important when interpreting weight and BMI within a population.

values.definition: Narrow bone structure; slight wrist and elbow.
Average bone structure.
Broad bone structure; thick wrist and elbow.

observability.notes: Better estimated from visible wrist/elbow when arms are bare; clothed assessment is approximate.

dimensions.scale_citation: Vague J (1956). The degree of masculine differentiation of obesities: a factor determining predisposition to diabetes, atherosclerosis, gout, and uric calculous disease. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 4(1): 20-34. Subsequent literature refined the gynoid/android distinction.
dimensions.description: Pattern of body-fat distribution. Independent dimension from BMI — two individuals with the same BMI can have very different distributions, with different cardiometabolic risk profiles.

values.definition: Fat accumulation predominantly in hips, thighs, and buttocks; lower-body distribution.
Fat accumulation predominantly in abdominal and visceral regions; upper-body distribution.
No strong upper-body or lower-body fat preference.
Fat accumulation predominantly in arms and legs rather than trunk.

dimensions.scale_citation: Qualitative scale aligned with sports-medicine training-status descriptors (Untrained, Recreationally Active, Trained, Highly Trained, World-Class) — Mann TN, Lamberts RP, Lambert MI (2013). Sports Medicine, 43(7).
dimensions.description: Visible musculature, ordinal. Captures training status and muscle hypertrophy as observable from photograph.

values.definition: Soft musculature; no visible definition; no evident strength training.
Slight musculature; some tone but no definition.
Visible muscle tone in major groups; some definition under good lighting.
Clear definition in major muscle groups; visible separation between groups.
Pronounced muscle mass and definition; evidence of sustained strength training.
Bodybuilder-class muscle mass; substantial volumetric hypertrophy.

observability.notes: Definition assessment requires visible musculature; clothed photographs allow only mass estimation.

dimensions.scale_citation: Cormic index = sitting height / standing height; population norms in Eveleth PB, Tanner JM (1990). Worldwide Variation in Human Growth, 2nd Edition. Cambridge University Press.
dimensions.description: Relative length of trunk versus legs. Anthropologically meaningful — varies systematically across populations, with East Asian populations averaging higher cormic indices (longer trunk relative to legs) and Sub-Saharan African populations averaging lower.

values.definition: Cormic index above population mean; trunk dominant.
Cormic index near population mean.
Cormic index below population mean; legs dominant.

dimensions.scale_citation: Kendall FP, McCreary EK, Provance PG (2005). Muscles: Testing and Function with Posture and Pain, 5th Edition. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.
dimensions.description: Habitual sagittal-plane postural alignment as visible from a side-view photograph. Postural deviations are common and meaningful for body-shape assessment.

values.definition: Vertical line through ear, shoulder, hip, knee, and ankle in side view.
Increased thoracic kyphosis and lumbar lordosis; head-forward posture.
Reduced lumbar lordosis; flattened lower spine.
Pelvis shifted forward of plumb; thoracic spine compensates posteriorly.
Head positioned anterior to shoulders without other major deviations.

observability.notes: Best assessed from a side-view photograph in habitual standing position; assessment from frontal-only views is unreliable.

dimensions.scale_citation: Cooke TD, Sled EA, Scudamore RA (2007). Frontal plane knee alignment: a call for standardized measurement. Journal of Rheumatology, 34(9): 1796-1801.
dimensions.description: Tibiofemoral alignment in the frontal plane. Absorbed from the original Knees atlas category. Varus and valgus alignment have systematic ethnic-group variation in the orthopedic literature.

values.definition: Tibiofemoral angle approximately 0° in the frontal plane (with normal physiologic valgus); knees and feet aligned.
Distal femur and proximal tibia angled medially; knees touch when feet apart.
Distal femur and proximal tibia angled laterally; gap between knees when feet together.
Asymmetric — one valgus, one varus.

observability.notes: Best assessed from frontal full-body view with feet together. Mild physiologic valgus is normal in adults; only deviations are flagged here.

dimensions.scale_citation: Qualitative descriptors for visible knee morphology; absorbed from the original Knees atlas category. No single canonical scale — descriptive vocabulary aligned with anatomic-anthropology usage.
dimensions.description: Visible morphology of the knee region as a soft-tissue silhouette.

values.definition: Wider, more boxy knee profile; pronounced patellar prominence within a broader soft-tissue envelope.
Smoother, more rounded knee profile; less distinct patellar outline.
Patella visible as a distinct elevated landmark even at rest.
Notable difference between left and right knee morphology.
